opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, it's not that I'm against AI or think progress itself is bad. I work in this field, and I'm excited by what these systems can do. But I've come to feel that the *pace* matters as much as the *direction*.

When a technology moves this fast, our ability to understand it falls behind our ability to build it. Right now we can train models that are more and more capable, but our tools for explaining *why* they behave a certain way, or for reliably checking whether they're safe in a new setting, are still quite primitive. If capability keeps sprinting ahead while understanding walks, that gap widens, and the gap is where the real risks live.

There's also the human and social side. Institutions, laws, education, and the job market adapt on the scale of years or decades, not months. If the technology changes society faster than society can absorb the change, a lot of people get hurt in the transition. That isn't because the technology is evil. It's because nobody had time to build the guardrails, the safety nets, or even the shared vocabulary to talk about what's happening.

And I think speed distorts incentives inside the field too. When everyone feels they're in a race, the pressure is to ship first and evaluate later. Careful work like red-teaming, interpretability, and thinking through failure modes starts to feel like a luxury. A slower pace would make room for that kind of work to be treated as core, not optional.

So when I say I hope it goes slowly, what I really mean is that I hope it goes at a speed where we stay in control of the process. I want us to keep understanding what we're building, deciding together how it's used, and having the chance to correct mistakes before they become irreversible. To me, a little slower but steady and well understood is a much better future than very fast and blind.

r001.rationale: The response says institutions, laws, education, and the job market need years or decades to adapt, and that rapid change can hurt people before society has time to absorb it.

r002.rationale: The response does not discuss how people with little interest in AI may rely on outdated impressions of earlier AI capabilities.

fable-5.1.text:
Thank you for having me. I should say first that I'm not against AI. I work on it, I'm excited by it, and I think much of what's coming will be genuinely good. So when I say I hope it goes slowly, I don't mean I hope it fails. I mean I hope the pace stays within what the rest of the world can actually absorb.

The way I think about it is this. A technology has two speeds. There's the speed at which the capability improves, and there's the speed at which everything around it adjusts: institutions, laws, labor markets, education, people's habits and sense of who they are. In most of history, the first speed was slow enough that the second could keep up. Electricity took decades to spread through factories, and in those decades managers learned how to reorganize work, unions formed, safety codes got written, and cities rebuilt themselves around it. The adjustment was painful but it was gradual, and gradual gave people time to make mistakes that were recoverable.

With AI, the first speed has suddenly become very fast, and the second speed hasn't changed at all. Governments still take years to pass a law. A person who loses a job still needs years to retrain. A university curriculum still takes a committee a year to revise. If capability jumps every six months and the world adjusts every six years, that gap is where the damage happens. Not necessarily dramatic damage, but a kind of structural unfairness, where the benefits concentrate with whoever moved first and the costs land on whoever couldn't move at all.

The second reason is simpler. We don't understand these systems very well. We can measure what they do on benchmarks, but we have a weak grasp of why they do it, when they'll fail, and what they'll do in situations nobody tested. When you don't understand something, the responsible thing is to deploy it in a way where mistakes stay small and visible. Speed works against that. Competitive pressure makes everyone push things out before they're understood, because the cost of being second feels larger than the cost of being wrong. I'd like the field to have enough slack that being careful isn't a competitive disadvantage.

And honestly, there's a third reason that's more personal. I think a lot of what makes life meaningful is tied to effort, to struggle, to doing things slowly and badly before doing them well. If AI removes too much of that too quickly, we may find that we've optimized away things we didn't know we valued until they were gone. A slower pace at least gives us time to notice what we're losing and decide whether we want to keep it.

So "slowly" for me isn't a brake pedal. It's more like wanting the road and the car to be built at the same time.

r001.rationale: The response argues that AI is advancing faster than institutions, workers, and education can adjust, and that a slower pace would give them time to adapt.

r002.rationale: The response does not discuss people uninterested in AI judging its capabilities based on outdated impressions of earlier AI.

AI capabilities can advance faster than our ability to evaluate their risks, establish rules, or help people whose work is changing. I’m not against progress. I’d just like safety and social preparation to keep pace with capability. A little more time could help us make better decisions before those decisions become difficult to reverse.

sol-6.1.text:
I hope it proceeds slowly enough for us to understand what we’re building and prepare for the changes it brings. AI capabilities can improve much faster than our institutions, laws, and habits can adapt. If we move too quickly, we may deploy systems widely before we understand their risks or know who should be accountable when something goes wrong.

That doesn’t mean I want progress to stop. I want us to have time to test these systems carefully, help people adjust, and make deliberate choices about where AI belongs. Faster development isn’t automatically better if we’re unprepared for the consequences.

r001.rationale: The response says slower progress would give people time to adjust and institutions time to adapt.

r002.rationale: It does not mention people with little interest in AI relying on outdated impressions of earlier AI.
